title: Chest pain that woke him at 1 a.m. and had almost settled

source.citation: Khalid WKK, Aziz ST, Ibrahim HAM, Zafar H. Atypical Posterior Myocardial Infarction With Minimal Symptoms: Diagnostic Impact of Point-of-Care Ultrasound. Cureus. 2026;18(4):e107446.

presentation.chiefComplaint: Intermittent chest discomfort for four days
presentation.hpi: Four days of intermittent chest discomfort. At about 01:00 today a severe episode (7/10) woke him from sleep, with sweating and nausea but no vomiting. By the time he reached the ED at 04:00 the pain had largely settled (1/10).
pmh: No diabetes, hypertension, chronic kidney disease or atrial fibrillation
presentation.social: Light smoker (fewer than 10 cigarettes a day). Physically active with regular gym attendance; BMI 22 kg/m², no central obesity.
presentation.family: No family history of premature cardiovascular disease.

imaging.modality: Point-of-care echocardiography in the ED (parasternal short axis)
imaging.finding: Regional wall motion abnormality: reduced systolic thickening and inward motion (hypokinesia) of the inferior/inferolateral wall
Hypokinesia of the basal to mid inferior and inferolateral walls

imaging.modality: Coronary angiography with optical coherence tomography
imaging.finding: Dominant right coronary artery (RCA) with a proximal lesion of moderate (50–74%) stenosis; OCT features of plaque erosion

ecg: 12-lead: about 1 mm ST depression in V1–V3 with relatively tall but non-dominant R waves (R/S < 1); T waves in V1 not upright. Posterior leads: ST elevation about 1 mm in V7 and V8 and 0.5 mm in V9.

diagnosis.primary: Posterior myocardial infarction (ST elevation in V7–V9) from a proximal right coronary artery lesion with plaque erosion
differentials: Non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction with anterior subendocardial ischemia

management: Aspirin and ticagrelor according to the local acute coronary syndrome protocol

On-call cardiology judged that the ECG did not meet traditional posterior MI criteria (ST depression < 2 mm, T in V1 not upright, R/S < 1); initial plan was local admission as NSTEMI rather than immediate transfer
Because of ongoing concern and the very high troponin, bedside POCUS in the ED; the regional wall motion abnormality led to re-contacting cardiology and escalation of care
Accepted for urgent transfer to a tertiary cardiac centre as posterior MI; ambulance arrived within about 10 minutes
PCI with a 3.5 × 28 mm drug-eluting stent to the proximal RCA, with final TIMI 3 flow
Discharged on secondary prevention with smoking cessation advice and cardiac rehabilitation referral
outcome: Clinically stable after PCI; discharged after two days on secondary prevention, with smoking cessation advice and referral to cardiac rehabilitation.
teachingPoints: ST depression maximal in V1–V3 can be the mirror image of posterior ST elevation: record V7–V9.
The report cites ESC criteria: ST depression ≥0.5 mm in V1–V3, particularly with ST elevation ≥0.5 mm in V7–V9, suffices; ≥2 mm depression, R/S > 1 and an upright T in V1 are not required.
Minimal residual pain may reflect spontaneous reperfusion; the culprit plaque remains unstable and can reocclude.
A troponin out of proportion to a 'non-diagnostic' ECG should prompt a search for an occluded artery.
On POCUS, a regional wall motion abnormality in the matching territory supports acute ischemia, but old infarcts look similar, so interpret it in context.

questions.q: What is the most useful next step to clarify this ECG?
questions.extra: 12-lead ECG: about 1 mm ST depression in V1–V3 with relatively tall but non-dominant R waves (R/S < 1); T waves in V1 not upright.
options: Repeat a standard 12-lead ECG in 3 hours
questions.explanation: ST depression maximal in V1–V3 may be the reciprocal image of posterior ST elevation, which posterior leads V7–V9 show directly. Right-sided leads look for right ventricular involvement in inferior STEMI, waiting 3 h delays a reperfusion decision, and stress testing is unsafe with possible ongoing infarction.

questions.q: How should this presentation now be classified?
questions.extra: Posterior leads: ST elevation about 1 mm in V7 and V8, 0.5 mm in V9. hs-troponin >1,000 ng/L (upper reference limit 14 ng/L).
options: NSTEMI for local admission and angiography within 72 hours
Type 2 myocardial infarction from supply–demand mismatch
Unstable angina with a non-diagnostic ECG
Posterior STEMI, an occlusion MI needing urgent reperfusion
questions.explanation: ST depression in V1–V3 with ST elevation ≥0.5 mm in V7–V9 (≥1 mm in men under 40, met here in V7–V8) is isolated posterior MI, which ESC guidelines list among STEMI-equivalent patterns that should prompt a primary PCI strategy. Classic features (≥2 mm depression, R/S > 1, upright T in V1) are not required; treating it as NSTEMI was the near miss here.

questions.q: Cardiology still favours local admission. Which bedside finding would most strongly support urgent transfer for angiography?
options: New inferior/inferolateral hypokinesia on point-of-care echo
A 5 mm pericardial effusion on point-of-care echo
A dilated right ventricle with septal flattening on echo
Bilateral diffuse B-lines on lung ultrasound
questions.explanation: Wall-motion abnormalities appear early in the ischemic cascade; hypokinesia in the territory matching the ECG, with a troponin above 1,000 ng/L, is direct evidence of ongoing ischemia and is what prompted escalation in this case. A dilated RV suggests PE and B-lines suggest pulmonary edema.

evidence.quote: A 39-year-old male patient with no significant past medical history and not on regular medications presented to the emergency department with intermittent chest discomfort over four days.
The pain was initially severe (7/10), waking him from sleep at approximately 1:00 AM … associated with diaphoresis and nausea, with no vomiting.
By the time of arrival at the emergency department at 4:00 AM, the pain had significantly improved, with a reported intensity of 1/10.
He was physically active, regularly attending the gym, with a body mass index (BMI) of 22 kg/m² and no evidence of central obesity.
He was a light smoker (<10 cigarettes/day) and non-diabetic and had no history of hypertension, chronic kidney disease, or atrial fibrillation.
There was no personal or family history of premature cardiovascular disease
On examination, he was haemodynamically stable

evidence.field: vitals.tempC, vitals.hr, vitals.sbp, vitals.dbp, vitals.rr, vitals.spo2
evidence.quote: temperature 36.8°C, heart rate 86 bpm, blood pressure 144/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air
Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations were unremarkable.
approximately 1 mm ST-segment depression in leads V1-V3 with associated tall R waves; however, the R/S ratio was <1, and T waves in V1 were not upright
Posterior leads (V7-V9) demonstrated ST elevation of approximately 1 mm in V7 and V8, and 0.5 mm in V9, supporting the diagnosis
Initial high-sensitivity troponin was markedly elevated (>1,000 ng/L; upper reference limit 14 ng/L).
The patient was treated according to local acute coronary syndrome protocol with aspirin and ticagrelor.
discussion with the on-call cardiology team concluded that the ECG did not fulfil traditional criteria for posterior MI
managed conservatively with local admission as NSTEMI, rather than immediate transfer for invasive management
due to ongoing clinical concern and the discrepancy between the markedly elevated troponin and the ECG appearance, bedside POCUS was performed in the emergency department
This demonstrated clear regional wall motion abnormalities involving the inferior/inferolateral wall, corresponding to the posterior myocardial territory on ECG
the cardiology team was re-contacted, and the presence of regional wall motion abnormalities prompted escalation of care
The patient was subsequently accepted for urgent transfer to a tertiary cardiac centre with a working diagnosis of posterior MI.
The ambulance arrived within approximately 10 minutes, and the patient was transferred promptly to the cardiac centre.
Formal transthoracic echocardiography performed at the cardiac centre confirmed hypokinesia of the basal to mid inferior and inferolateral walls.

Coronary angiography demonstrated a dominant right coronary artery with a proximal lesion showing moderate (50%-74%) stenosis. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) identified features consistent with plaque erosion.
The patient underwent successful percutaneous coronary intervention with deployment of a 3.5 × 28 mm drug-eluting stent, achieving final TIMI 3 flow
The patient remained clinically stable post-procedure and was discharged after two days with appropriate secondary prevention, smoking cessation advice, and referral to cardiac rehabilitation.
